summary: The fleet can now keep its own copy of the footage that matters, off the appliance. A new per-rule 'Keep a fleet copy' flag on a mymatasan detection rule (default off) marks the alerts whose evidence must survive the recorder being stolen, burned, submerged or wiped by whoever set off the alarm — the failure modes that destroy the recording of the very event it is evidence of, and the one case that retention, tamper detection and continuity monitoring all assume cannot happen. When such a rule fires, the flag rides upstream with the alert; the control plane queues the clip, waits for the node to finish cutting it, then pulls it over the existing mutual-TLS control tunnel in bounded byte ranges, hashes the bytes as they arrive, and stores the footage and its snapshot encrypted at rest beside the incident record. A new read-only /api/clips surface lists what the fleet has kept and plays it back with seeking, publishing the digest so a recipient can verify the copy; every viewing is written to the audit trail, because once the fleet holds a copy the appliance's own trail can no longer answer who watched it. Deliberately narrow: nothing is archived unless a rule was explicitly flagged, since a control plane holding every clip from every camera is a storage problem pretending to be a security feature. Deliberately careful too — a clip that arrives short is refused rather than stored (a truncated video still plays, so nothing downstream would ever notice the missing thirty seconds with the incident in them), a snapshot is kept only if it really is an image, a clip the fleet was asked to keep and could not raises an alert rather than failing quietly, and an archive that reaches its size limit stops and says so rather than deleting older evidence to make room.
compatibility: Purely additive and off by default: no rule archives anything until an operator ticks the new checkbox, so an upgraded fleet behaves exactly as before. One new table (archived_clip) and one new column on the node's detection_rule arrive through the normal auto-migrator with no manual migration. Nothing about detection, recording, alerting or notification delivery changes; the flag is stamped only onto the control plane's copy of an alert and never leaks into webhook or chat payloads. The archive is NOT part of .selbackup and this is deliberate — that bundle is a control-plane configuration backup, and rows without their gigabytes of media would restore into a list of incidents whose footage is missing, which is worse than listing nothing; back the clip directory up with the data directory. Archived media is kept 90 days, the archive is capped at 20 GB, and reaching the cap stops archiving with an operator alert rather than evicting anything. Fetching asserts the fleet's operator role on the node (a viewer has no recording access at all, and reading a clip needs no write authority). Live-benched against a real fleet with real footage — a control plane and two adopted nodes on the real mTLS control channel, a camera recording a live RTSP stream — 22/22, including the product claim itself: after the clip was archived the node was destroyed and its data directory wiped, and the footage still played back from the control plane byte-identical to the digest taken as it arrived, with the node and camera still named on the record. Also verified end to end: an unflagged rule's alert is not archived; an alert raised while the control plane was DOWN is archived when it reconnects; and unauthenticated reads are refused. That bench found and fixed one defect: an alert raised without an image caused the node's JSON refusal to be stored as the clip's 'snapshot'.
